title: Mastery Challenge: US History
objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of US History Levels 1 to 99 across the whole tree.
summary: Questions from across the tree: first peoples, colonies, revolution, the republic, a house divided, war, Reconstruction, industry and how historians argue.

cards.headline: The US History Mastery Challenge.
cards.body: Questions from across the whole tree, from the first Americans to how historians argue. Level 1 asked how an old land became a young nation; now see how much of that story you can tell. Take your time: every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: US History: mastered
learned: How Native nations, enslaved people, women and immigrants shaped the American story, not only its presidents.
Why slavery drove secession and the Civil War, and how Reconstruction’s promise was won and lost.
What separates a fact from an interpretation, and how to weigh historians’ rival explanations.
Which questions to ask of any source, from Douglass’s 1852 speech to a popular myth.

questions.prompt: Why did epidemics hit Native nations so hard after 1492?

options.label: The Americas had none of Eurasia’s crowd diseases, so no one had met them
Native people had no doctors or medicine
options.rationale: Native nations had their own healers; the problem was germs no one had met.

options.label: Europeans spread disease on purpose everywhere they went
options.rationale: Epidemics spread largely without anyone planning them.

options.label: The climate of the Americas made every disease worse
options.rationale: The cause was new germs, not the climate.

questions.explanation: Before 1492 the Americas had none of the acute infectious diseases, such as smallpox and measles, so populations fell by 50 to 95 percent by 1650.

questions.prompt: The SlaveVoyages database estimates how many Africans were forced aboard ships to the Americas?

options.label: About 388,000
options.rationale: That is about how many were landed in mainland North America.

options.label: About 1.8 million
options.rationale: That is roughly how many died on the way.

options.label: About 10.7 million
options.rationale: That is about how many survived the crossing.

options.label: About 12.5 million

questions.explanation: SlaveVoyages estimates about 12.5 million were forced aboard and about 10.7 million survived.

questions.prompt: What persuaded France to openly ally with the United States in 1778?

options.label: The Boston Tea Party
options.rationale: That was a protest in 1773.

options.label: News of the American victory at Saratoga
The Declaration of Sentiments
options.rationale: That was written at Seneca Falls in 1848.

options.label: The Treaty of Paris
options.rationale: That treaty ended the war in 1783.

questions.explanation: News of Saratoga persuaded France’s foreign minister to choose an open alliance, signed on February 6, 1778.

questions.prompt: Why does the election of 1800 matter so much in American history?

options.label: It was the first peaceful transfer of power from one party to another
It was the first election women could vote in
options.rationale: Women won the national vote in 1920.

options.label: It made Washington president
options.rationale: Washington was elected in 1789.

options.label: It ended the Articles of Confederation
options.rationale: The Constitution replaced the Articles earlier.

questions.explanation: In 1800 power passed peacefully from Adams’s Federalists to Jefferson’s Republicans for the first time.

questions.prompt: The Supreme Court ruled for the Cherokee in Worcester v. Georgia (1832). What happened next?

options.label: Georgia returned all Cherokee land
options.rationale: Georgia ignored the ruling.

options.label: Congress repealed the Indian Removal Act
options.rationale: The Removal Act stayed in force.

options.label: Georgia ignored the ruling, and President Jackson declined to enforce it
The Cherokee moved west that same year
options.rationale: Forced removal came in 1838.

questions.explanation: Georgia ignored the ruling and Jackson declined to enforce it: a court can decide, but someone else has to act.

questions.prompt: The Emancipation Proclamation took effect in 1863. In which places did it leave slavery untouched?

options.label: Everywhere in the Confederacy
options.rationale: It declared freedom in areas in rebellion.

options.label: In the loyal border states and Confederate areas the Union already held
Only in Washington, DC
options.rationale: The DC slave trade had ended in 1850; the Proclamation didn’t single out DC.

options.label: Nowhere: it ended slavery everywhere
options.rationale: The 13th Amendment ended slavery everywhere later.

questions.explanation: It applied only to areas in rebellion, leaving slavery untouched in the loyal border states and Union-held Confederate areas.

questions.prompt: How did the Dawes Act of 1887 cost Native nations most of their land without a battle?

options.label: It moved every nation to Oklahoma
options.rationale: That was not what the Dawes Act did.

options.label: It banned Native people from farming
options.rationale: It pushed Native families to farm allotments.

options.label: It gave the land to railroads
options.rationale: It sold leftover land to non-Native settlers.

options.label: It split reservations into allotments and sold the “surplus” to settlers

questions.explanation: Reservations were split into 160-acre allotments, the leftover land sold; holdings fell from about 138 million acres to about 48 million by 1934.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest evidence for why the Deep South seceded in 1860 and 1861?

options.label: Lost Cause books written after the war
options.rationale: Those came after defeat, and historians largely consider them false.

options.label: Modern opinion polls
options.rationale: Polls show what people think today, not why states left.

options.label: The seceding states’ own declarations of causes
Longfellow’s poems
options.rationale: Longfellow wrote poetry, not secession records.

questions.explanation: The declarations were written by the decision-makers at the time, and several named the defense of slavery.

questions.prompt: Whose 1935 book challenged the Dunning School’s verdict that Reconstruction was a mistake?

options.label: W. E. B. Du Bois
William A. Dunning
options.rationale: Dunning founded the school Du Bois challenged.

options.label: Carl Becker
options.rationale: Becker wrote about the Revolution in 1909.

options.label: Henry Stimson
options.rationale: Stimson defended the atomic bombings in 1947.

questions.explanation: Du Bois’s Black Reconstruction (1935) showed freedpeople actively shaping Reconstruction.

questions.prompt: Parson Weems added the cherry tree story to his book in 1806, after Washington died. How should a historian treat it?

options.label: As a primary source, because Weems knew Washington’s family
options.rationale: Nothing from the time backs the story.

options.label: As a myth: no record from the time supports it
As a fact, because millions of students read it
options.rationale: Popularity is not evidence.

options.label: As a secondary source that settles the question
options.rationale: A later, unsupported story settles nothing.

questions.explanation: Weems invented the story years after the fact; with no primary source behind it, it is a myth.
